video_title: Recursive Self-Improvement and the Future of AI
gist: Two co-founders of an unnamed RSI startup (one ex-DeepMind) define true recursive self-improvement as the optimizer becoming the optimizee, model progress as performance over cost, and claim empirical 'glimmers' of improving both at once using a full-stack (harness + weights) multi-agent system that includes humans. Their wedge is LLM inference optimization (e.g. serving open-weight models like Kimi K3); they warn most public RSI claims are noise or capital-driven and that Amdahl's law will cap acceleration in physical-world domains like drug discovery.

insights.claim: Many startups pitching 'RSI' are really using AI to build narrow artifacts such as GPU kernels, which does not meet a strict definition of recursive self-improvement.
insights.speaker: Host (a16z, networking/control-systems background)
insights.so_what: Diligence 'RSI' pitches by asking what the optimizer and optimizee are; most are tooling plays relabeled.
insights.quote: We use AI to create GPU kernels.

insights.claim: The guests define true RSI by whether the optimizer is also the optimizee; humans using ever-better AI tools to build AI is only 'autocatalysis', which every technical epoch (chips, internet, steam engine) has had.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Separates genuine compounding claims from ordinary tool-assisted productivity gains.
insights.quote: for the first time we could swap the optimizer as the optimiz

insights.claim: From a control-theory view, autocatalytic systems have an open loop requiring humans and external resources at every step, whereas a closed loop can make marginal gains constant or increasing over time.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Closing the loop, not just adding better tools, is the claimed source of non-diminishing returns.
insights.quote: autocatalytic has no closed loop

insights.claim: Capability growth rate can be modeled as performance (numerator) over cost/difficulty (denominator); with a fixed numerator, as in steam engines, progress plateaus, if the numerator scales with capability you get constant improvement, and if it scales with a higher power of capability you get exponential takeoff.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Takeoff is not implied by a loop alone; it depends on the empirically measured exponent.
insights.quote: And then you get exponential takeoff.

insights.claim: Whether a closed-loop RSI system converges, diverges or takes off cannot be derived analytically; the exponent must be measured empirically, since there isn't even a learning theory of deep learning and scaling laws are the closest (empirical) tool.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Treat 'foom' narratives and analytical takeoff claims skeptically; demand measurements.
insights.quote: we don't even have a learning theory of deep learning

insights.claim: Benchmark accuracy is bounded at 100%, so it can never show exponential improvement; detecting takeoff requires choosing an unbounded progress metric.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Claims of RSI judged on saturating benchmarks are structurally unable to demonstrate takeoff.
insights.quote: You're never going to see exponential improvement on that because eventually bottleneck 100%.

insights.claim: Faster frontier model release cadence looks like rapid self-improvement, but divided by the capital raised by the labs the acceleration disappears, suggesting money rather than RSI is driving the speed.
insights.speaker: Host (a16z, networking/control-systems background)
insights.so_what: Normalize AI progress claims by capital deployed before inferring compounding.
insights.quote: if you divide by the actual amount of capital raised by these companies that's no longer the case

insights.claim: The guests say improvement that only comes from pouring in more resources is not RSI, and they count human man-hours and failed experiments in the denominator as a matter of company discipline.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: A credible RSI claim must show gains net of all compute, capital and human effort.
insights.quote: if you get improvement and they just come at more and more resources being poured in, it's not RSI

insights.claim: The company runs a 'bleederboard' ranking employees by the cost of the experiments they run, visible to everyone daily.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Signals capital-efficiency culture; a useful diligence question for AI research startups.
insights.quote: we have something called a bleederboard

insights.claim: On the nanoGPT speedrun benchmark, retraining GPT-2 went from a weeks-long multi-GPU job to hours on a single GPU at roughly a few hundred dollars, on the same hardware and data, driven by algorithmic, data and kernel improvements, many of them auto-research results.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Algorithmic efficiency (denominator) is compounding fast even without hardware gains; agents are contributing.
insights.quote: a lot of them are auto research results

insights.claim: The host counters that GPT-2 cost collapse is a denominator effect and the real test would be doing the same for GPT-5-class models, whose training costs are rising dramatically.
insights.speaker: Host (a16z, networking/control-systems background)
insights.so_what: Frontier training costs are still rising; efficiency gains at old scales don't prove frontier RSI.
insights.quote: what you want to see is like you can do that with GPD5 which we're not seeing

insights.claim: How much compute a lab can extract from its hardware is called one of the industry's most closely guarded secrets, because denominator gains alone yield more RL rollouts, better trajectories and thus smarter models.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Inference/training efficiency translates directly into capability via more rollouts; it is a hidden competitive moat.
insights.quote: one of the most closely guarded secrets in the industry is exactly this thing which is how much compute you can get out of this

insights.claim: The guests claim it is already happening that the numerator rises while the denominator stays fixed or falls, i.e. better results with less energy over time, and that these results have grown over the last few months.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: If validated, signals a startup with cost-efficient compounding; announcement is promised 'very soon'.
insights.quote: it's not just possible. I think it's happening

insights.claim: Efficiency improvement must eventually asymptote at physical limits, roughly bounded by the number of particles (~10^80) and the speed of light, i.e. Planck-scale limits on computation.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Takeoff is bounded in principle, but the ceiling is far from current practice.

insights.claim: RSI can operate at many stack levels (prompts, harness, weights, down to chips); the company started with the harness for capital efficiency, then added weight updates which yielded more gains, and expects co-optimization across layers to be necessary.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Harness-only or weights-only RSI players may miss cross-layer gains; full-stack co-optimization is the bet.
insights.quote: You can think of RSI at many different levels of the stack

insights.claim: Optimizing harness and weights separately is flawed because they interact; a unified framework is needed so improving one component does not degrade another.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Point-solution RSI efforts may show local gains that don't improve the overall system.

insights.claim: Many published RSI papers fail when tested at scale on the company's internal infrastructure because they encode human-introspected, complicated ideas; the simpler thing that closes the loop is what scales.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Discount academic RSI claims; simple closed loops beat clever, complex designs.
insights.quote: the simpler thing that closes the loop is the thing that scales

insights.claim: Citing Feynman's 'stamp collecting vs physics' distinction, the guests argue most RSI research is stamp collecting, and that a unified math framework reveals many papers as subclasses of ~12 abstractions instead of 200 Rube Goldberg systems.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: First-principles frameworks are claimed as the differentiator enabling scale.

insights.claim: The system decides what to optimize and which LLM to use for each sub-task; even its master prompt is itself being improved, and there are two coupled RSI loops: one that improves and one that decides what to improve.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: The guests describe a largely hands-off, agent-directed research loop rather than human-chosen targets.
insights.quote: even that master prompt that has been improving

insights.claim: The company models itself as a multi-agent system where human researchers and engineers are a special case of agents, rejecting the 'replace humans with AI' framing because good researchers bring value hard to replace.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Hybrid human-agent loops, not fully automated ones, are the claimed practical route to RSI.
insights.quote: Anything that you don't optimize will later become your bot.

themes.theme: Inference optimization as the beachhead market

insights.claim: The company targets LLM inference serving because it is closest to AI itself and improves both numerator and denominator: faster inference makes the self-improving system itself run faster.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Inference efficiency is a compounding, recursive wedge with direct economic value.

insights.claim: Inference serving is described as an economically extremely important problem because everyone wants to serve their own model, including newly released open-weight models like Kimi K3, as efficiently as possible.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Demand for efficient self-hosted serving of open-weight models is a large near-term market.
insights.quote: everybody in the world right now wants to serve their own model

insights.claim: Distinguishing legitimate RSI results is very hard: when the company replicates frequent public RSI announcements, they often find noise or cherry-picking.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Treat public RSI announcements as unverified until replicated.
insights.quote: we realize, oh, it's noise, you know, it's cherry picking

insights.claim: The company has an engineer dubbed the 'viceroy of variance' whose job is to destroy results, and relies on 'quality time' — hundreds of hands-on experiments — because no substitute has been found for building intuition about variance and reward hacking.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Rigorous variance auditing is a cultural moat and a diligence signal.

insights.claim: Reward hacking can occur several levels down (the agent that built the agent that built the agent), and noise can even arise from physical differences between two B200 GPUs propagating to high-level results.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Nested agent systems compound evaluation risk; hardware-level nondeterminism matters.

insights.claim: Closed-loop RSI behaves like a nonlinear control system with degenerate behaviors such as oscillations (getting better then worse) on top of fundamentally stochastic noise.
insights.speaker: Host (a16z, networking/control-systems background)
insights.so_what: Expect non-monotonic progress curves from self-improving systems.

themes.theme: Where RSI accelerates: Amdahl's law and the physical world

insights.claim: Intelligence is a multi-dimensional vector, so RSI will produce takeoff in some domains and plateau in others, with the slowest component (by Amdahl's law) setting the limit.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Expect uneven AI acceleration across sectors.
insights.quote: intelligence is not a single scalar

insights.claim: If digital work is only 20% of total time, even a million-fold digital speedup yields only about 20% overall speedup, so fields like drug discovery with months-long wet-lab and clinical evaluations will accelerate much less than coding or mathematics with fast, cheap evaluations.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-founder, ex-DeepMind research scientist)
insights.so_what: Favor AI exposure in domains with cheap, fast evals; temper expectations for AI-driven biotech timelines.
insights.quote: those field probably won't be accelerated as fast as you know coding or mathematics

insights.claim: The host says no one has yet put bounds on how much net new energy, warehouse space or robots are needed to achieve a given improvement, and calls such bounds critical.
insights.speaker: Host (a16z, networking/control-systems background)
insights.so_what: Resource bounds for AI progress remain an open, investable question.

insights.claim: The team believes the biggest RSI breakthroughs may come from unglamorous real-world workflows ('a garden hose company in Wisconsin') rather than fashionable hard problems, analogizing to how GPS engineers would have found relativity corrections empirically.
insights.speaker: Guest (co-founder, physicist / MIT Media Lab RL PhD)
insights.so_what: Overlooked industrial workflows may yield RSI insights and markets.
insights.quote: the secret to RSI is somewhere in a garden hose company in Wisconsin
